chapters.title: Lesson 1 · Observing Celestial Phenomena and the Way of the I Ching

lessons.title: Lesson 1 · Observing Celestial Phenomena and the Way of the I Ching
lessons.description:
**Introduction**

Since ancient times, leaders of all generations have emphasized observing celestial phenomena and deducing the movements of the sun, moon, and stars. During the Five Emperors and Three Dynasties, this knowledge flourished. The Chinese regarded themselves as the center and treated foreign peoples as peripheral. Above, they observed the starry heavens; below, they modeled the patterns of earthly things.

---

**The Way of Heaven and Earth**

Heaven has the sun and moon; earth has yin and yang. Heaven has the five planets (Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, Venus, Mercury); earth has the five elements (wood, fire, earth, metal, water). Heaven has its constellations; earth has its boundaries. The ancient sages could synthesize the affairs of heaven and earth, analyzing and reasoning through symbolic imagery.

---

**Ancient Astronomers vs. Modern Meteorology**

In ancient times, several sages transmitted the science of heaven, known as the "Heavenly Officials". These were like today's meteorological stations, but similar in form yet different in spirit. Modern weather stations only report changes in celestial phenomena and analyze climate, and their forecasts are often inaccurate after the event. They may know beforehand, but cannot prevent or make long-term predictions. Thus, humanity is still beset by natural disasters, unable to avoid them in advance, able only to remedy them afterward.

---

**Astrology and the Human Heart**

The most advanced astrology today knows only that the stars and constellations exert gravitational influence on Earth, but not that this influence reaches human hearts and penetrates every aspect of human life. Humanity blindly passes its days, lingering between power and wealth, not knowing it is but a speck of sand in the vast universe. Obsessed and unawakened, people rejoice at small gains, and when slightly prosperous, disregard laws and discipline. Society worships wealth; hearts become corrupt, and right and wrong are no longer distinguished.

---

**The Wisdom of the I Ching**

Today, we particularly present the great wisdom of the ancient sages. The I Ching says: "The superior man serves heaven; the small man serves other men." This is a warning to all the small men of the world. Now is the beginning of peril and decline. We urge everyone to follow goodness as naturally as water flows. When good and evil are distinguished, the way of the superior man returns, and a world of order arrives.

---

**The Cycles of Heavenly Destiny**

Ancient records describe the cycles of heavenly destiny: thirty years bring a small change; a hundred years, a medium change; five hundred years, a great change. Three great changes form one era; three eras complete a full cycle of four thousand five hundred years. Those who govern must observe the thirty-year small changes and examine the preceding millennium. Only then can the relationship between heaven, earth, and humanity become complete in accordance with heavenly destiny. Those who govern in harmony with heaven prosper; those who defy heaven perish.

---

**The Five Planets and Twenty-Eight Constellations**

The stars in heaven have been traditionally divided into five major sections, called the "Five Palaces". The constellations number twenty-eight, distributed across the four directions: east, south, west, and north. This discourse discusses not only the matters governed by each constellation but also the relationships between the sun, moon, and five planets (the "Seven Governments") and the twenty-eight constellations, thereby inferring their influence on Earth and humanity. Not only can worldly changes be known from the celestial signs, but because we know the beginning of events, we can prevent the emergence of calamities.

---

**The Wisdom of the Ancient Sages**

This approach differs from modern scholars' research methods. People today often investigate after the event, but when harm has already been done, no amount of money can repair it. Therefore, I have excerpted the celestial phenomena from ancient texts to correspond with the situations of today's world. May all descendants of the Yellow Emperor and Yan Emperor feel proud to be part of the Chinese nation, and in the leisure after meals and tea, deeply appreciate the wisdom of the ancient sages and philosophers.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 · What Is the I Ching?
lessons.description:
**Lesson 2: What Is the I Ching?**

The Way of Change in Harmony with Heaven, Lesson 2

**Introduction**

Many people have heard of the I Ching, yet relatively few truly understand it.

Some regard it as a book of divination, some associate it with feng shui, and others classify it as a form of mysticism.

The intellectual and philosophical scope of the I Ching, however, extends far beyond these interpretations.

Mr. Nan Huaijin regarded the I Ching as a living wellspring of Chinese culture.

Professor Fu Peirong has emphasized that the I Ching is concerned not merely with favorable or unfavorable outcomes, but with human life itself.

Professor Zeng Shiqiang likewise observed that the purpose of studying the I Ching is not simply to predict the future, but to understand the patterns of change.

We study the I Ching, therefore, not to become preoccupied with speculations about fate, but to understand enduring principles, cultivate wisdom, and gain insight into the Dao of human life.

Learning unfolds at different levels.

At the elementary level, one acquires knowledge; at the intermediate level, one masters methods; at the advanced level, one perceives underlying principles.

The I Ching explores the fundamental patterns through which the universe, society, and human life unfold and change.

---

**I. What Does “Yi” Mean?**

To understand the I Ching, we must begin with the meaning of the Chinese character “Yi.”

Scholars throughout Chinese history have often explained “Yi” through three interconnected meanings: change, simplicity, and constancy.

**The First Meaning: Change**

All things between Heaven and Earth are in a continual process of change.

The seasons follow one another in recurring cycles; economies rise and decline; organizations grow and transform; and family relationships evolve through different stages of life.

Human thought, understanding, and conduct likewise change with experience and circumstance.

One of the most common difficulties in life arises when we confront a changing world with an unchanging mindset.

Some people grow through change because they are willing to observe reality and adapt themselves accordingly.

Others gradually fall into difficulty because they remain attached to the past and resist necessary transformation.

The I Ching thus reminds us that all things are continually changing, and that change itself is one of the most enduring realities of existence.

**The Second Meaning: Simplicity**

The greatest truths are often expressed through the simplest principles.

Although the phenomena of the universe are extraordinarily complex, the fundamental principles behind them are not necessarily obscure.

What we sow largely determines what we harvest.

Sustained effort generally contributes to growth.

Long-term accumulation often prepares the way for breakthroughs.

Consideration for others, together with integrity in action, generally helps to build trust.

These principles may appear simple, yet they form an important foundation for human life and social relationships.

A common problem in modern life is the tendency to make simple matters unnecessarily complicated.

One form of wisdom offered by the I Ching is the ability to see fundamental principles beneath complex appearances and to respond with clarity and simplicity.

**The Third Meaning: Constancy**

Within change, there are also enduring patterns that remain relatively constant.

The seasons continually succeed one another, yet the cyclical order of the four seasons endures.

The forms of business continually evolve, yet value creation remains essential to the survival of any organization.

Times continue to change, yet the fundamental needs and emotions of human beings do not disappear.

Tools are constantly renewed, yet the relationship between actions and consequences remains.

The I Ching therefore studies not only change, but also guides us in recognizing the enduring principles that operate within change.

The ability to discern constancy amid continual transformation is one of the central expressions of the wisdom of the I Ching.

---

**II. Why Is the I Ching Called “The First Among the Classics”?**

Within the traditional Chinese intellectual system, the I Ching has long occupied a position of exceptional importance.

Through centuries of compilation and interpretation, the Confucian canon came to include the collection known as the “Thirteen Classics.”

The I Ching stands prominently among them and has traditionally been honored as “the first among the classics” and “a source of the Great Way.”

This is because many classical works have their own particular areas of concern, whereas the I Ching focuses on change itself and the universal principles underlying it.

The Analects is primarily concerned with moral cultivation and proper conduct in human relationships.

The Great Learning emphasizes self-cultivation and the relationship between the individual, the family, and the wider social order.

The Doctrine of the Mean develops the wisdom of balance, harmony, and appropriate action.

The Dao De Jing explores naturalness, non-coercive action, and the relationship between humanity and the Dao.

The Art of War focuses on strategic judgment, the assessment of circumstances, and the principles of conflict.

The I Ching investigates the general patterns of change that run through nature, society, and human life.

The ancients valued the I Ching because medicine, military leadership, scholarship, and social governance all require several fundamental abilities: observing change, assessing trends, and recognizing the right moment for action.

These abilities lie at the heart of the enduring value of the I Ching.

---

**III. The True Subject of the I Ching**

Many people assume that the I Ching is primarily concerned with events that have not yet occurred.

Its deeper significance, however, lies in understanding how reality operates and why things change.

From the perspective of traditional Chinese philosophy, the concerns of the I Ching may be summarized as the Way of Heaven, the Way of Earth, and the Human Way.

**The Way of Heaven**

The Way of Heaven refers to the patterns governing nature and the cosmos.

The movements of the sun and moon, the succession of the seasons, the cycle of day and night, and the waxing and waning of yin and yang may all be understood as expressions of the Way of Heaven.

To understand the Way of Heaven is not to seek control over nature, but to observe larger tendencies and respect the rhythms of the natural world.

**The Way of Earth**

The Way of Earth refers to patterns within the natural environment, geographical conditions, available resources, and the wider social setting.

The same choice may produce different results when made under different conditions.

To understand the Way of Earth is to recognize the conditions in which one lives and to discern both their limitations and possibilities.

**The Human Way**

The Human Way refers to the fundamental patterns of personal development, human relationships, and social life.

Personal growth, marriage, career, and family life are not isolated individual events, but outcomes of the continuing interaction between the individual, other people, and society.

To understand the Human Way is to understand human nature, human feeling, and responsibility, while seeking an appropriate sense of measure in relationships.

The fundamental framework of the I Ching can therefore be understood as the interconnection of the Way of Heaven, the Way of Earth, and the Human Way.

An understanding of the Way of Heaven helps us perceive trends; an understanding of the Way of Earth helps us assess circumstances; and an understanding of the Human Way helps us understand people.

Only by considering all three together can we make wiser choices in complex situations, move toward favorable conditions, and reduce avoidable risks.

---

**IV. One of the Central Ideas of the I Ching: Yin and Yang**

Yin and yang form an essential foundation for understanding the thought of the I Ching.

Ancient Chinese thinkers used yin and yang to describe complementary and interdependent forces or states within nature and human society.

Day and night, movement and stillness, firmness and gentleness, advance and retreat, opening and closing may all be understood through the relationship between yin and yang.

Yin and yang are neither completely separate nor absolute opposites that can only reject one another.

They are distinct yet interdependent; they restrain one another, yet also enable one another to flourish.

Without night, life would have no time for rest; without reflection, action may easily lose its direction.

A business must create products, but it must also understand its customers; a leader must make decisions, but must also listen to the people within the organization.

Family relationships likewise require a balance of firmness and gentleness, together with mutual respect.

The wisdom of yin and yang does not require the elimination of all differences. Rather, it asks us to understand and harmonize differences, allowing distinct forces to fulfill their proper functions within a balanced relationship.

Mature wisdom is concerned not merely with winning or losing in the moment, but with establishing enduring balance and harmony.

---

**V. The First Lesson the I Ching Offers Modern Life**

Many difficulties in modern life arise from a failure to recognize change in a timely manner.

Career stagnation, entrepreneurial difficulty, and strained family relationships do not always result from a lack of effort. Sometimes they arise because former assumptions and methods no longer correspond to present conditions.

**Change in the Workplace**

When an industry undergoes structural transformation, complete dependence on past experience may cause a person’s abilities to become increasingly disconnected from present needs.

Experience itself is not a burden, but experience that is never examined or renewed may become a limitation.

**Change in Entrepreneurship**

When market demand has changed but products, services, and business practices remain fixed in the past, the risk of failure naturally increases.

Entrepreneurship requires not only perseverance, but also attentiveness to the market, the testing of assumptions, and timely adjustment.

**Change in Family Life**

As children grow, the relationship between parents and children must evolve accordingly.

If parents continue to use the same methods of communication and instruction that they used in early childhood, they may overlook the child’s developing independence and thereby create continuing conflict.

These examples show that although effort is important, direction and method are equally important.

If we continue to rely on an outdated map, we may fail to understand a world that has already changed.

The I Ching therefore reminds us that changing one’s life often begins with changing one’s understanding.

Only when understanding changes can behavior be adjusted; and only when behavior changes consistently can the direction of life gradually be transformed.

---

**VI. The Principal Benefits of Studying the I Ching**

Through systematic study, we may gradually develop a way of thinking grounded in change, relationships, and timing.

This way of thinking may be expressed through five principal abilities.

**The First Ability: Perceiving Trends**

People often focus on isolated events, whereas the I Ching encourages us to observe the relationships among events.

Events are outward manifestations; recurring structures and directions of change may reveal deeper patterns.

To perceive a trend is not to predict the future with certainty, but to understand possible directions of development on the basis of observable change.

**The Second Ability: Knowing When to Advance and When to Withdraw**

Not every moment in life is suitable for rapid advance.

At times we must act with initiative, and at times with caution; at times we should move quickly, and at times we should wait patiently.

Knowing when to advance and when to withdraw is not passive retreat. It is the ability to understand timing and align action with actual conditions.

**The Third Ability: Making Discerning Choices**

Effort alone cannot guarantee the achievement of every goal.

When direction remains misaligned with circumstance, greater investment may sometimes lead only to greater cost.

What matters is not merely working harder, but discerning what deserves persistence, what requires change, and what should be released at the appropriate time.

**The Fourth Ability: Understanding People**

People differ in personality, experience, perspective, and need.

Understanding these differences does not mean accommodating others without principle. It means communicating more accurately and conducting relationships with a proper sense of measure.

Understanding people is essential to the wise management of family, organizational, and social relationships.

**The Fifth Ability: Cultivating One’s Life**

Life requires thoughtful cultivation, but cultivating life does not mean controlling every aspect of it.

It means clarifying the direction of one’s work, sustaining harmony within the family, and preserving inner steadiness amid change.

External conditions may continually change, but through learning, reflection, and practice, a person can gradually establish a stable inner order.

---

**Core Principles of This Lesson**

Keep the following four statements in mind:

The I Ching is not merely a method of divination, but a discipline for understanding change.

Its purpose is not to make absolute claims about the future, but to perceive the patterns through which events unfold.

It does not lead us toward superstition or obscurity, but encourages the cultivation of wisdom.

It is not an escape from reality, but a guide to facing life with greater clarity.

---

**Reflections After the Lesson**

Sit quietly for ten minutes, set aside the noise of the outside world, and reflect carefully on the following three questions.

Question 1: What significant changes have taken place in your life over the past five years?

These changes may have arisen in your work, family, health, or relationships, or in the way you understand yourself and the world.

Question 2: What recurring patterns can you identify behind these changes?

Consider which choices have produced similar outcomes, which emotions have led to repeated behaviors, and which environmental factors have continued to influence you.

Question 3: If you continue with your present way of thinking and acting for the next five years, where might your life be heading?

This question does not ask you to predict the future. It invites you to recognize how the choices of today may shape the direction of tomorrow.

---

**Summary of Lesson 2**

The first step in studying the I Ching is to clarify a common misunderstanding.

The value of the I Ching does not lie merely in telling people what may happen in the future.

More importantly, it helps us understand why events occur, how they change, and how we should respond after change has taken place.

Beginning today, we may establish the first principle of I Ching thought.

**The First Principle of the Philosophy of Change**

Observe change without fearing it.

Act in accordance with underlying principles rather than against them.

Understand the conditions of the time rather than attempting to force them.

Make wise use of favorable timing rather than moving against it.

“Favorable timing” does not refer to a mysterious force, but to the objective conditions, stages, and opportunities present within the development of events.

By observing change, we reduce blindness; by respecting underlying principles, we avoid reckless action; and by recognizing the right moment, we allow our efforts to produce better results.

This is the first key to the course The Way of Change in Harmony with Heaven.

In the next lesson, we will examine the three meanings of “Yi”: change, simplicity, and constancy, and formally enter the central framework of I Ching thought.

chapters.title: Lesson 3 · The Principle of Yin and Yang: Two Dimensions of Every Situation

lessons.title: Lesson 3 · The Principle of Yin and Yang: Two Dimensions of Every Situation
lessons.description:
**Lesson 3 The Principle of Yin and Yang: Two Dimensions of Every Situation**

**Introduction**

If Change is the living spirit of the I Ching, Simplicity its method, and Constancy its foundation, then yin and yang provide one of its essential keys to understanding the world.

The Commentaries on the Changes state: “The successive movement of yin and yang is called the Dao.” This does not simply divide the world into two separate realms. Rather, it describes how the alternating, interacting, and changing relationship between yin and yang expresses the underlying Way through which things unfold.

To study yin and yang is not to pursue mystical knowledge, but to cultivate a way of observing relationships, understanding differences, and recognizing change.

Many difficulties in life arise not only from events themselves, but also from our tendency to judge them in absolute terms: black or white, right or wrong, good or bad.

The principle of yin and yang reminds us that reality is often more complex than simple either-or judgments. Apparently opposing forces may depend on one another, and seemingly contradictory factors may form parts of a single process.

The principle of yin and yang does not deny conflict or erase the distinction between right and wrong. It helps us recognize relationships within difference, seek coordination amid opposition, and maintain dynamic balance through change.

---

**I. What Are Yin and Yang?**

Yin and yang are not two fixed, concrete entities. They are philosophical concepts used to describe relative relationships between things, forces, states, or tendencies.

In different contexts, traditional Chinese thinkers used such relationships as moon and sun, night and day, gentleness and firmness, stillness and movement, inner and outer, preservation and advance, and Earth and Heaven to illustrate yin and yang.

These correspondences are not permanently fixed, nor do they signify superiority and inferiority, nobility and baseness, good and evil, or differences in human worth.

The same thing may be described as yin in one relationship and as yang in another. Yin and yang must therefore be understood according to particular relationships and conditions.

One of the most important characteristics of yin and yang is that they are opposed yet complementary.

Without night, we could not clearly distinguish day; without stillness, movement could not be defined; and without consolidation, expansion might lose the foundation required for continuity.

Failure may be painful, yet it can reveal our limitations and encourage reflection. Success deserves appreciation, yet it may also bring the risks of pride, complacency, or poor judgment.

The I Ching therefore considers not only how two forces oppose one another, but also how they depend upon, complement, regulate, and transform one another.

---

**II. Four Fundamental Patterns of Yin and Yang**

**The First Pattern: Relativity and Opposition**

Many things contain two distinct or even opposing dimensions.

Entrepreneurship may create opportunity, but it also involves risk. Marriage may offer intimacy and support, while also requiring responsibility and adjustment. Leadership brings a degree of authority, but also greater pressure and accountability. Wealth expands one’s choices, yet may create new concerns involving preservation, distribution, and responsibility.

People are often attracted to the brighter and more appealing side of a situation while overlooking the conditions, responsibilities, and costs that accompany it.

When reality fails to match our expectations, disappointment and anxiety may arise.

Mature thinking asks not only, “What can I gain from this?” but also, “What responsibilities must I assume, and what costs must I accept in order to gain it?”

Only by seeing opportunity and risk, rights and responsibilities, benefits and costs together can we make more comprehensive and prudent judgments.

**The Second Pattern: Mutual Dependence**

The mutual dependence of yin and yang means that each relies upon the other and that neither can be fully understood or sustained in complete isolation.

The familiar taiji diagram presents black and white forms embracing one another, each containing a small circle of the opposite color. It visually expresses the idea that there is yang within yin and yin within yang.

The image reminds us that things rarely exist in an absolutely pure or isolated form.

Success may contain the seeds of failure, while failure may contain the conditions for a new beginning.

When a business is performing well, pride, complacency, or excessive expansion may gradually turn success into risk.

When a business encounters difficulty, a careful reassessment of its products, management, and capacity for innovation may turn hardship into the beginning of transformation.

This does not mean that every failure will automatically lead to success, or that every success must inevitably end in failure.

Mutual dependence means that every situation may contain different possibilities of development, while the eventual outcome depends on specific conditions and on human understanding, choice, and action.

We therefore need not become overconfident at good news or fall immediately into despair at bad news. What matters more is calmly observing the conditions that are already present or beginning to emerge.

**The Third Pattern: Waxing and Waning**

Yin and yang are not static. They are engaged in a continual process of waxing and waning.

As one tendency grows stronger, the other may become relatively weaker. When the direction of development changes, what was previously weaker may gradually become stronger.

The length of day and night waxes and wanes with the seasons. A longer day does not literally become night, but day and night change in relative proportion within daily and seasonal cycles.

Human life likewise unfolds through different stages. Youth may bring greater physical energy; middle age may strengthen experience, judgment, and responsibility; and later life may bring the distinctive value of accumulated insight.

Each stage has its own strengths and its own limitations.

The waxing and waning of yin and yang reminds us that we need not prove our worth in the same way at every stage of life, nor should we regard temporary strength or weakness as a permanent conclusion.

The I Ching does not encourage an endless struggle to rank first. It encourages continuing growth based on an understanding of one’s stage of life and actual circumstances.

Momentary brilliance may not endure, while stable and sustainable development often carries greater value.

**The Fourth Pattern: Transformation**

Yin and yang are not only opposed, interdependent, and continually waxing and waning. Under certain conditions, they may also transform into one another.

When a tendency continues to develop and reaches a certain limit, the original condition may undergo a qualitative transformation.

Traditional Chinese culture uses expressions such as “when adversity reaches its limit, favorable conditions may return,” “extremes may turn into their opposites,” “the full moon begins to wane,” and “water overflows when the vessel is full” to remind us of the changes that may occur when a condition reaches an extreme.

Chapter 58 of the Dao De Jing states: “Misfortune is that upon which good fortune depends; good fortune is that within which misfortune lies concealed.” The passage expresses the idea that favorable and unfavorable conditions are interrelated and may, under certain circumstances, transform into one another.

Transformation, however, is not an automatic process independent of conditions. Setbacks do not naturally become opportunities, nor does success turn into crisis without cause.

Human attitude, judgment, and action often influence the direction of transformation.

The wisdom of transformation does not encourage passive waiting. It asks us to remain vigilant in favorable circumstances and to seek actions that can change conditions in times of adversity.

---

**III. Yin-Yang Thinking and Self-Cultivation**

**The First Level: Accepting and Understanding Oneself**

Many people suffer because they are willing to accept only their strengths and cannot tolerate their limitations.

In reality, the strengths and limitations of a personality trait often arise from the same underlying tendency.

Caution can make a person thoughtful and dependable, but excessive caution may cause opportunities to be missed.

Decisiveness can improve efficiency, but decisiveness without sufficient judgment may become impulsiveness.

Enthusiasm can inspire and encourage others, but without emotional regulation, it may lead to overreaction.

Patience can support long-term perseverance, but excessive waiting may become hesitation when prompt action is required.

Self-cultivation does not simply mean eliminating what we call our weaknesses. It means understanding our characteristics, developing their constructive potential, and preventing them from becoming excessive.

True growth does not require becoming someone else. It requires learning to use one’s own capacities with greater awareness.

**The Second Level: Understanding and Regulating Emotion**

Emotions cannot be divided simply into categories of right and wrong.

Anger may alert us that a boundary has been violated; fear may warn of potential danger; sadness may help us process loss; and joy may strengthen connection and vitality.

The problem usually lies not in the emotion itself, but in whether we understand the information it carries and choose an appropriate way to express it.

Yin-yang balance does not mean suppressing all emotion, nor does it require a person to appear calm at all times.

It means neither being completely controlled by emotion nor denying its presence, but creating appropriate space between feeling, understanding, and action.

The ability to recognize emotion, accept it, and regulate one’s behavior is an important part of self-cultivation.

**The Third Level: Balancing Firmness with Gentleness**

The I Ching places importance on the coordination of firmness and gentleness.

Firmness involves principle, courage, and the capacity for action. Gentleness involves listening, adaptation, and openness to different views.

Firmness without gentleness may become harshness, while gentleness without firmness may lead to the loss of one’s position or boundaries.

A mature person knows when to stand firm and when to adjust, how to express principles clearly, and how to communicate them in a manner others can receive.

Traditional Chinese culture often describes this wisdom as being “rounded on the outside and square within.”

Being “square within” means preserving principles and boundaries; being “rounded on the outside” means expressing them with flexibility and tact.

External flexibility does not mean insincerity, nor does inner firmness mean stubbornness. Together, they represent a balance between principle and method.

---

**IV. Yin-Yang Thinking and Family Relationships**

**Partnership**

Many disagreements between partners arise not solely from the issue itself, but because both sides wish to prove themselves right and expect the other person to accept their perspective completely.

A family relationship is not a debate in which the objective is to defeat the other person.

From the perspective of yin and yang, a healthy partnership requires coordination between different functions, such as action and listening, exploration and preservation, decision and mediation, independence and companionship.

These functions should not be assigned rigidly according to gender.

In modern family life, both partners may share financial responsibility, care for the household, make decisions, and provide emotional support according to their abilities, preferences, and actual circumstances.

What matters is not deciding who must represent yang and who must represent yin, but ensuring that the family has both the energy to move forward and the capacity to preserve stability and connection.

Partners do not need to be identical, but they should learn to understand differences, share responsibilities fairly, and support one another in pursuit of common goals.

**Parent-Child Relationships**

Family education likewise requires coordination between openness and discipline, trust and boundaries.

If parents are excessively strict, children may become suppressed, fearful, or deprived of autonomy under continuing pressure.

If parents provide no meaningful boundaries, children may struggle to develop responsibility, self-management, and appropriate limits.

Good education does not mechanically choose between strictness and permissiveness. It adjusts its approach according to the child’s age, personality, and circumstances.

Principles should be clear, while their expression may remain gentle. Rules should be stable, while their application should leave room for understanding and communication.

Balancing care with discipline is one expression of yin-yang thinking in family education.

---

**V. Yin-Yang Thinking and Professional Development**

**Act with Resolve and Treat Others with Respect**

In the workplace, completing a task generally requires clear objectives, effective execution, and timely decisions.

These qualities may be understood through yang because they express initiative, clarity, and outward movement.

Professional cooperation also requires listening, respect for others, coordination, and openness to difference.

These qualities may be understood through yin because they express receptiveness, adjustment, and the preservation of relationships.

A mature professional attitude may therefore be summarized as follows: act with determination, and treat others with humility and respect.

When professional development is obstructed, lack of technical ability may not be the only reason. Excessive self-promotion, disregard for the contributions of others, or an overly competitive attitude may also prevent the formation of lasting trust.

Ability should be recognized, but it should not be displayed at the cost of diminishing others or damaging cooperation.

**Ability and Cooperation**

Professional development requires both individual ability and healthy working relationships.

Ability enables a person to create value, while cooperation allows that value to be sustained within an organization.

Focusing on ability while neglecting communication may prevent a person from gaining necessary support. Relying on relationships without competence is equally unlikely to establish lasting professional credibility.

Sound professional development requires both character and competence, together with independent judgment and the ability to work with others.

This is another expression of balancing firmness with gentleness.

---

**VI. Yin-Yang Thinking in Entrepreneurship and Business**

Entrepreneurs may place great emphasis on expansion while neglecting protection, pursue growth while overlooking risk, or enlarge operations without sufficient attention to cash flow and organizational capacity.

Expansion, growth, and outward movement display yang characteristics. They can create opportunities, open markets, and promote development.

Risk management, cost control, cash reserves, and internal governance display yin characteristics. They help an organization preserve its strength, withstand uncertainty, and maintain order.

A business that focuses only on defense without innovation may gradually lose competitiveness. A business that pursues expansion without controlling risk may enter a crisis after a period of rapid growth.

Some businesses do not fail during their most difficult period, but after achieving initial success, when overconfidence, uncontrolled expansion, or insufficient managerial development begins to create problems.

This may be understood as an excess of yang and an insufficiency of yin: outward growth has exceeded the organization’s internal capacity.

Sound management requires dynamic coordination between the following:

Growth and profitability.

Innovation and stability.

Speed and quality.

Vision and reality.

Market expansion and internal governance.

Short-term opportunity and long-term value.

Balance does not mean that both sides must always receive an equal share. It means making appropriate adjustments according to the organization’s stage of development, resources, and environment.

A new venture may initially require greater emphasis on exploration, while later stages may require stronger systems, quality control, and risk management.

Yin-yang balance is not a static average. It is a dynamic order that continually adjusts as circumstances change.

---

**VII. From Choosing One Side to Coordinating Relationships**

A widely used modern summary of yin-yang thought suggests that when facing a complex problem, we should not rush to choose one side, but should first seek an appropriate relationship among the different factors involved.

This idea can be illuminating, but it should not be turned into an absolute distinction between “Chinese thinking” and “Western thinking.”

Across different cultural traditions, we find approaches that emphasize logical analysis, moral judgment, holistic relationships, balance, and dialectical change.

The distinctiveness of I Ching thought does not lie in rejecting judgments of right and wrong. It lies in considering relationships, conditions, timing, and consequences when making those judgments.

Some situations require clear moral judgment and accountability. The language of balance must not be used to avoid principle.

Other situations may have no single correct answer and require negotiation, adjustment, and mutual complementarity to reach a more appropriate solution.

The wisdom of yin and yang does not seek compromise in every situation. It asks us to determine when to stand firm, when to adjust, when to cooperate, and when to establish a clear boundary.

The question is not only how to win, but how to endure; not only how to move faster, but how to remain stable; not only how to become stronger, but how to develop together with others.

---

**Core Principles of This Lesson**

Keep the following eight Chinese characters in mind:

Balance firmness with gentleness, and know the proper measure of advance and retreat.

They may be further summarized as follows:

Act in accordance with changing conditions without moving toward extremes.

Maintain dynamic balance and continue to grow.

Here, balance does not mean remaining motionless, nor does it require all forces to remain permanently equal.

True balance is a continual adjustment according to timing, position, relationships, and actual conditions, allowing different forces to regulate and support one another.

---

**Practice**

Write the third entry in your Journal of Life and the Way of Change, taking one day to observe your thoughts, emotions, and behavior.

The purpose of this exercise is not to label yourself permanently as yin or yang, but to recognize your present behavioral tendencies and how they influence your life.

**Question 1: What Is the Most Evident Yang Tendency in My Character?**

For example, do you display strong decisiveness, competitiveness, initiative, expressiveness, or capacity for action?

In what situations have these qualities helped you? Under what circumstances might they become excessive?

**Question 2: What Is the Most Evident Yin Tendency in My Character?**

For example, are you cautious, accommodating, sensitive, attentive, inclined to listen, or given to careful reflection?

What value have these qualities brought you? Under what circumstances might they restrict your action?

**Question 3: What New Conditions May Be Found Within My Greatest Setback of the Past Year?**

Did this setback reveal a limitation, encourage you to learn a new ability, change your understanding of a relationship, or lead you to reconsider your direction?

Do not rush to reinterpret the setback as something positive. Instead, carefully identify those factors within it that may genuinely support growth.

**Question 4: What Risks May Be Hidden Within My Greatest Success of the Past Year?**

Has this success encouraged pride, complacency, excessive expansion, or a tendency to disregard the views of others?

What abilities, relationships, or safeguards should you strengthen now in order to make this success more sustainable?

---

**Lesson Summary**

The I Ching teaches that yin and yang cannot be understood in isolation. A later expression summarizes this relationship by saying, “Yin alone cannot generate, and yang alone cannot sustain growth.” This fixed formulation appears in the Youth’s Primer and should not be quoted as a direct passage from the I Ching.

Wisdom in life does not lie in becoming permanently stronger than everyone else. It lies in recognizing our strengths and limitations and maintaining appropriate coordination in different circumstances.

Yang may symbolize the powers of creation, action, exploration, and expression.

Yin may symbolize the powers of receptiveness, preservation, accumulation, and adjustment.

Development without preservation may lose its foundation, while preservation without innovation may gradually harden into stagnation.

The harmony of yin and yang does not eliminate difference. It allows distinct forces to interact within an appropriate relationship and contribute together to development.

From this, we may establish a basic framework for reflection and decision-making:

When observing a situation, consider its different dimensions.

When taking action, understand the measure and timing of advance and retreat.

When managing relationships, consider principle, difference, and coordination together.

When facing success, recognize the risks that may be emerging within it.

When facing adversity, seek actions that can change the conditions of the situation.

True yin-yang wisdom sees different sides without falling into relativism, seeks balance without abandoning principle, and understands change without waiting passively.

---

**Preview of the Next Lesson**

Lesson 4 The Way of the Supreme Ultimate: A Framework for Moving from Complexity to Order

In the next lesson, we will explore an important starting point in the cosmology and symbolic framework of the I Ching.

The original passage in the Commentaries on the Changes reads: “In the Changes there is the Supreme Ultimate. From it arise the Two Modes; from the Two Modes arise the Four Images; and from the Four Images arise the Eight Trigrams.”

The phrase “Non-Ultimate and yet the Supreme Ultimate” comes from the Northern Song thinker Zhou Dunyi’s Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate. It is not part of the original passage in the Commentaries on the Changes. A published edition should clearly distinguish these two formulations and their historical sources.

Through the generative relationship among the Supreme Ultimate, the Two Modes, the Four Images, and the Eight Trigrams, we will learn how to break down a complex problem step by step and identify fundamental structures beneath diverse appearances.

This framework can assist us in analyzing problems, developing strategies, and planning our lives by connecting broad direction with concrete action.

**Lesson 4 The Way of Taiji: A Model for Moving from Complexity to Order**

**Introduction**

In the first three lessons, we explored the three meanings of Yi and the patterns behind change. We also studied yin and yang and learned how different forces interact and balance one another.

This leads to a natural question: Where do yin and yang come from?

The Commentaries on the Changes state:

“In the Changes there is Taiji. From Taiji arise the Two Modes; from the Two Modes arise the Four Images; and from the Four Images arise the Eight Trigrams.”

This is the classical account of how Taiji, the Two Modes, the Four Images, and the Eight Trigrams are related. It also forms an important foundation of the symbolic system of the Zhouyi.

The Two Modes are usually understood as yin and yang. They may also represent Heaven and Earth, firmness and gentleness, or other related pairs.

If yin and yang help us understand relationships, Taiji helps us understand how differences and structures emerge from a whole.

In this lesson, we will not treat Taiji as a mysterious symbol. Nor will we present ancient philosophy as modern science.

Instead, we will use it as a thinking model: begin with the whole, identify key relationships, determine the stage of development, and then build a clear structure.

In this sense, Taiji thinking is the ability to create order.

---

**I. What Is Taiji?**

When many people hear the word “Taiji,” they first think of taijiquan, or tai chi.

Taijiquan was influenced by the ideas of Taiji, yin and yang, movement and stillness. Taiji itself, however, is an important concept in Chinese philosophy.

The Commentaries on the Changes state: “In the Changes there is Taiji. From it arise the Two Modes.”

In English, Taiji may be translated as the Supreme Ultimate. This book mainly uses the Chinese term Taiji to preserve its cultural meaning.

Chinese scholars have understood Taiji in different ways. Some saw it as an original state of unity. Others saw it as the principle behind all things. Still others explained it through the formation of lines and trigrams.

Taiji should not be understood as a particular physical substance.

In this course, Taiji refers to a whole before its inner structure has fully unfolded. It contains possibilities that have not yet taken clear form.

A seed contains the possibility of a future tree, but it is not yet the tree itself.

A strategy contains the basic direction of a company, but it must still be organized, carried out, and adjusted.

A life goal can focus a person’s attention and resources, but it cannot replace long-term action.

These examples are modern comparisons. They help explain Taiji, but they do not fully define its classical meaning.

Taiji is not an isolated “thing.” It is a philosophical idea about unity, differentiation, and development.

---

**II. Non-Ultimate and Yet Taiji**

In his Explanation of the Diagram of Taiji, the Northern Song thinker Zhou Dunyi wrote: “Non-Ultimate and yet Taiji.” He then explained that movement gives rise to yang, stillness gives rise to yin, and movement and stillness depend on each other.

“Non-Ultimate and yet Taiji” is not the same statement as “In the Changes there is Taiji.” The first comes from Song-dynasty philosophy, while the second comes from the Commentaries on the Changes.

Historical versions of the text use different opening phrases. The commonly received version reads, “Non-Ultimate and yet Taiji.”

**What Is Wuji?**

Wuji may be translated as the Non-Ultimate.

Here, “non” does not simply mean nothingness, and “ultimate” does not mean a physical endpoint.

In Song-dynasty philosophy, Wuji points to what has no fixed form or boundary. It is not a physical object.

For modern readers, Wuji may be compared to an open state without a fixed direction or clear structure.

A recent graduate may have many possible paths.

The person may enter education, business, art, technology, or public service.

At this stage, many possibilities remain open. Life has not yet formed a clear center.

This can serve as a simple life metaphor for Wuji.

**From Wuji to Taiji**

When a person finds a clear purpose, scattered possibilities begin to gather around a center.

For example, the person may choose medicine, entrepreneurship, or education.

From that point, time, knowledge, relationships, and resources begin to move in one direction.

Other possibilities do not disappear completely, but life now has a clearer center.

In this modern comparison, Wuji represents the open state, while Taiji represents an emerging whole with a clear center.

This is not a strict classical definition. It is a way to understand the movement from the undefined to the defined, and from scattered energy to focus.

---

**III. From Taiji Arise the Two Modes**

The Two Modes usually refer to yin and yang.

When a whole begins to unfold, different forces, directions, and functions appear.

Movement and stillness, firmness and gentleness, advance and retreat, opening and closing can all help us understand the Two Modes.

The Two Modes are not two separate worlds. They are two relative forces within one whole.

**The Two Modes in Business**

A business usually contains two related kinds of energy.

Market development, innovation, sales growth, and expansion move outward. They may be understood through yang.

Finance, risk control, processes, and internal governance protect and organize the business. They may be understood through yin.

Expansion without management may exceed the company’s capacity.

Management without innovation may cause the company to lose energy and competitiveness.

The Two Modes remind us that lasting development usually requires different forces to work together.

**The Two Modes in Family Life**

Family life also contains relationships that must be balanced.

A family needs effort and rest, boundaries and understanding, personal growth and mutual support.

These roles should not be fixed by gender or assigned permanently to one person.

Family members can share duties according to ability, preference, and actual conditions.

The key is not deciding who represents yin or yang. The key is whether the family has complementary strengths.

---

**IV. From the Two Modes Arise the Four Images**

In the symbolic system of the Zhouyi, yin and yang lines combine to form four two-line patterns. These are commonly called Young Yang, Old Yang, Young Yin, and Old Yin.

This book uses the following terms:

- Young Yang (少阳)
- Old Yang (老阳)
- Young Yin (少阴)
- Old Yin (老阴)

The Four Images have been explained in different ways. They may refer to line patterns, divination numbers, the four seasons, or other symbolic systems.

Linking Young Yang, Old Yang, Young Yin, and Old Yin with spring, summer, autumn, and winter is a common interpretation. It is not the only meaning of the Four Images.

From the view of the seasons:

Young Yang suggests rising energy and may be linked with spring.

Old Yang suggests strong yang energy and may be linked with summer.

Young Yin suggests rising yin energy and may be linked with autumn.

Old Yin suggests strong yin energy and may be linked with winter.

This model shows that development does not happen all at once. Things emerge, grow, mature, decline, and begin again.

---

**V. Using the Four Images to Understand Life Stages**

We can use the Four Images as a simple model for stages of development.

The following stages are a modern application used in this course. They are not the only classical meaning of the Four Images.

**Stage 1: Emergence**

Emergence may be understood through Young Yang.

Something has just begun. Its direction is forming, but its strength and resources are still limited.

The main task is not rapid expansion. It is learning, testing, and building a foundation.

**Stage 2: Growth**

Growth may be understood through Old Yang.

Energy is stronger, opportunities increase, and development becomes faster.

This is the time to use opportunities. It is also important to avoid overexpansion and overconfidence.

**Stage 3: Maturity**

Maturity may be understood through Young Yin.

Growth may slow down. The existing model becomes stable, and internal problems become easier to see.

The main tasks are improving structure, raising quality, and preparing for future change.

**Stage 4: Transition**

Transition may be understood through Old Yin.

The old model is losing strength. Methods that once worked may no longer be useful.

The task is to learn from experience, reduce waste, and find a new direction.

Transition does not always mean a final ending. Winter appears quiet, but it preserves energy for new growth.

**A Career Example**

A person entering a new field is in the stage of emergence.

The person needs to learn basic knowledge, understand the rules, and build professional habits.

When the person becomes a strong contributor and gains influence, the career enters a period of growth.

After becoming a manager, the focus may move from personal tasks to team development, resources, and systems. This may be seen as maturity.

When old skills no longer meet new needs, or career growth stops for a long time, a period of transition may begin.

The person may need to learn new skills, take on a new role, or choose a different direction.

If we do not understand our stage, we may expand before we are ready or hold on to the past when change is needed.

This is part of what the I Ching means by understanding timing and one’s present stage.

---

**VI. From the Four Images Arise the Eight Trigrams**

Yin and yang lines combine into three-line figures. These form the Eight Trigrams: Qian, Kun, Zhen, Xun, Kan, Li, Gen, and Dui.

The Discussion of the Trigrams links the Eight Trigrams with Heaven, Earth, Thunder, Wind, Water, Fire, Mountain, and Lake. It also describes them through qualities such as strength, receptiveness, movement, penetration, danger, brightness, stillness, and joy.

The keywords below are modern applications based on classical images. They are not direct translations from the classical text.

**Qian ☰, the Creative**

**Natural image:** Heaven.

**Classical quality:** Strength.

**Modern keywords:** creation, leadership, purpose, direction.

Qian reminds us to act with initiative and clear purpose.

**Kun ☷, the Receptive**

**Natural image:** Earth.

**Classical quality:** Receptiveness.

**Modern keywords:** support, inclusion, service, execution.

Kun reminds us to stay grounded and turn ideas into reality through steady action.

**Zhen ☳, the Arousing**

**Natural image:** Thunder.

**Classical quality:** Movement.

**Modern keywords:** beginning, action, breakthrough, awakening.

Zhen reminds us to overcome hesitation and take the first step.

**Xun ☴, the Gentle**

**Natural image:** Wind.

**Classical quality:** Penetration.

**Modern keywords:** communication, spread, influence, gradual progress.

Xun reminds us that lasting influence may grow through gentle and steady communication.

**Kan ☵, the Abysmal**

**Natural image:** Water.

**Classical quality:** Danger or difficulty.

**Modern keywords:** risk, difficulty, adaptation, resilience.

Kan reminds us to face risk and find a path through difficulty.

**Li ☲, the Clinging**

**Natural image:** Fire.

**Classical quality:** Attachment, brightness, and visibility.

**Modern keywords:** insight, learning, culture, clarity.

Li reminds us to seek clarity through learning and understanding.

**Gen ☶, Keeping Still**

**Natural image:** Mountain.

**Classical quality:** Stillness or stopping.

**Modern keywords:** boundaries, restraint, focus, reflection.

Gen reminds us that we should not always keep moving. Knowing when to stop is also wisdom.

**Dui ☱, the Joyous**

**Natural image:** Lake or marsh.

**Classical quality:** Joy.

**Modern keywords:** dialogue, cooperation, relationships, joy.

Dui reminds us to build connections through honest dialogue and cooperation.

---

**VII. Applying the Eight Trigrams to Life**

Before studying the Sixty-Four Hexagrams, we can treat the Eight Trigrams as eight ways of looking at a situation, not as fixed personality types.

A person may need the initiative of Qian in one situation and the support of Kun in another.

When we feel lost, Li reminds us to learn and seek clarity.

When we lack action, Zhen reminds us to begin with one small step.

When we face difficulty, Kan reminds us to assess risk, stay resilient, and adapt.

When we become overconfident or expand too quickly, Gen reminds us to set limits and pause.

When we lack support, Dui reminds us to improve communication and relationships.

When we have ideas but lack execution, Kun reminds us to return to practical work.

When we lose direction, Qian reminds us to define our purpose again.

When others cannot understand our ideas, Xun reminds us to communicate more clearly and patiently.

The Eight Trigrams are not eight separate answers. They are eight resources for thinking in different situations.

---

**VIII. The Practical Value of Taiji Thinking**

As a modern application, Taiji thinking can be organized as a process that moves from the whole to a clear structure.

**Step 1: See the Whole**

First understand the background, scope, and main goal. Do not judge the whole situation from one sign.

**Step 2: Identify the Main Forces**

Identify the forces affecting the situation, such as growth and risk, stability and freedom, or speed and quality.

This is similar to identifying the yin-yang relationship within the whole.

**Step 3: Identify the Stage**

Ask whether the situation is emerging, growing, maturing, or changing direction.

Different stages require different actions.

**Step 4: Study the Structure**

Study the issue through goals, people, resources, processes, risks, communication, and environment.

The Eight Trigrams can offer different viewpoints for this analysis.

**Step 5: Make an Appropriate Decision**

Choose the action that best fits the goal, main tension, present stage, and actual conditions.

This may be seen as a modern use of I Ching thought in systems analysis. It should not be presented as the direct source of modern systems science.

**A Business Example**

A company finds that its sales are falling.

Looking only at the result, management may blame the sales team.

Taiji thinking asks us to see the whole and then study each level.

Has market demand changed?

Does the product still create value for customers?

Are the price and competitive strategy still suitable?

Does the team understand customer needs?

Is the brand message clear?

Does the business strategy still fit current conditions?

The company may find that falling sales are only the visible result. The deeper cause may be outdated product positioning.

Beginning with the whole, identifying relationships, understanding the stage, and finding structural causes is one way to apply Taiji thinking in management.

---

**IX. Addressing Problems Before They Grow**

Many problems in life and management are easier to address when they first appear.

A small issue, if ignored, may gradually affect more relationships and structures.

A small misunderstanding may grow into lasting distrust. A short cash-flow problem may become a business crisis. Long-term exhaustion may affect work, family, and judgment.

It is important not only to solve serious problems, but also to notice early signs and act before the problem grows.

This does not literally mean that an early problem is “in a Taiji state.” Taiji is a philosophical concept and should not be treated as a technical term for an early-stage problem.

More accurately, Taiji thinking teaches us to study the whole and the source before a conflict becomes more complex.

Chinese tradition often values prevention before a problem becomes serious. In modern life, this means finding risks early, building safeguards, and acting in time.

Prevention does not mean fearing the future. It means making small changes to avoid greater loss.

---

**Core Principles of This Lesson**

Remember this classical sequence:

In the Changes there is Taiji; from it arise the Two Modes.

From the Two Modes arise the Four Images.

From the Four Images arise the Eight Trigrams.

For modern life, it may be summarized as follows:

First see the whole, then identify the relationships.

Recognize the stage and study the structure.

Find the source and act at the right time.

---

**Practice**

Write the fourth entry in your Journal of Life and the Way of Change.

Choose one problem that you most want to solve and study it through the following steps.

**Question 1: What Is My Greatest Concern at Present?**

Describe the problem clearly in one or two sentences. Do not write only “anxiety,” “confusion,” or “too much pressure.”

For example:

I do not know whether to stay in my current job or enter a new field.

**Question 2: What Forces Are Shaping the Problem?**

For example:

Income and interest.

Stability and freedom.

Family responsibilities and career growth.

Risk and opportunity.

Short-term reward and long-term value.

Do not choose one side too quickly. First understand the need behind each side.

**Question 3: What Stage Has the Problem Reached?**

Has it just appeared? Is it growing? Has it become stable? Or has it reached a point where change is necessary?

Using the Four Images, is it closer to Young Yang, Old Yang, Young Yin, or Old Yin?

**Question 4: What Is the Root Cause?**

Ask “Why?” five times about the issue you see.

For example:

Why am I unhappy with my job?

Because I see no room for growth.

Why is there no room for growth?

Because my work has not changed for a long time.

Why has the work not changed?

Because I have not sought new projects or learned new skills.

After several questions, “the company gives me no opportunity” may become a clearer issue: “I have not actively created or sought new opportunities.”

The goal is not to blame yourself. It is to separate what you can change from what you cannot control.

---

**Lesson Summary**

Taiji is not simply a mysterious symbol or the name of a martial art.

It is an important Chinese philosophical idea about unity, difference, relationships, and development.

In the classical sequence, Taiji represents the whole. The Two Modes show its first division. The Four Images develop this division, and the Eight Trigrams form a richer symbolic structure.

As a modern thinking model, it offers four lessons:

Every development has a background and a source.

A whole often contains different interacting forces.

Different stages require different actions.

Complex events may have an underlying structure.

Understanding Taiji does not mean judging everything from one sign.

“To see autumn in a single leaf” means noticing a trend through small signs. It does not mean making careless predictions without evidence.

A mature thinker is not easily misled by appearances or controlled by temporary emotions and short-term gains.

Such a person first sees the whole and studies the relationships, then understands the stage and decides how to act.

Understand the foundation before deciding how to act.

This is another key through which the I Ching helps us cultivate wisdom for life.

---

**Preview of the Next Lesson**

Lesson 5 The Eight-Trigram Model: Understanding Yourself and the World

In the next lesson, we will begin our study of the Eight Trigrams.

We will explore the classical images, basic qualities, and modern uses of Qian, Kun, Zhen, Xun, Kan, Li, Gen, and Dui.

The Eight Trigrams can help us view personality, behavior, professional ability, organizations, and circumstances from different angles.

The Eight Trigrams do not divide people into eight fixed types.

Personality and behavior are shaped by temperament, experience, environment, and personal choice. The same person may show different trigram qualities in different situations.

The Eight-Trigram Model is a tool for seeing more clearly. It is not a system for placing fixed labels on people.

Through the next lesson, we will begin to build a personal I Ching map for life.
